Lab 2 — Vibe Coding: Plotly and Dash Interactive Visualization / Structuring a Narrative

By the end of this lab you will be able to:

  • Understand the workflow of Vibe Coding
  • Create a visualization plan before coding
  • Generate a data visualization application
  • Evaluate generated results and improve a dashboard through iteration
  • Structure a narrative for your data visualizations

We will continue using:

  • winemag-data-with-year.csv
  • wine_category.csv

Part 1 - Making a Dashboard by Vibe Coding

Traditionally, we write code first and then test the result.

With Vibe Coding, you describe what you want, and the AI generates the code.

Your role becomes:

  1. Define the problem
  2. Create a plan
  3. Review the AI’s proposal
  4. Test the result
  5. Improve the design

The idea matters more than the code.

For this lab, you could use any vibe coding tool (Cursor, Claude Code, Github Copilot…)

1. Create a Workspace Folder

Create a new workplace folder, for example, web_visualization.

Create a data folder and put the dataset files into it.

Open the folder in your vibe coding tool.

2. Create a Plan

Before generating any code, create a plan.

Write something about what visualization you want to build and implementation requirements:

I want to build a web dashboard to help users easily discover wine choices based on country, variety, price, and rating.

Requirements:

- Use Plotly and Dash
- Create a Python virtual environment using venv
- Understand data first. Data is stored in data/

- Include two to three interactive visualizations
- Include useful filtering options
- Use a map for country-based selection

Create a detailed implementation plan.

For Cursor: choose Plan New Idea
For Claude Code: press shift+tab and switch to plan mode on
For Github copilot: set agent to Plan

3. Review the Plan

Read the proposed plan carefully.

Consider questions such as:

  • Does it include all the visualizations I would like to draw?
  • Is there anything missing? (data, environment, visualization…)

These are only examples. Think critically about your own design and discuss additional improvements with the AI.

Do not rush into code generation. Modify the plan until you are satisfied. Spending a few minutes refining the plan often leads to a much better dashboard.

4. Generate the Application

After finalizing the plan, ask AI to implement it.

Example:

Follow the plan to implement.

Run the application and test the dashboard.

5. Evaluate and Improve

Manually review the dashboard and see if any improvements needed. Think of questions such as:

  • Are the visualizations meaningful?
  • Is the layout easy to use?
  • Are there too many charts?
  • Are important filters missing?
  • Would a wine beginner understand the dashboard?

Talk with AI using natural language and improve the dashboard iteratively if needed.

There is no single correct solution. Different people may create different dashboards.


Part 2 - Structuring a Narrative for Your Data Visualizations: An Introduction

As you can see, AI could generate the visualizations within minutes. What is the value of you, as humans, in the data visualization process? (Another way to re-phrase this question: How you can get better grade in the project?)


One key is the ability of wrapping up your findings into a narrative (i.e. Storytelling). A narrative in data visualization means

  • The process of combining charts and graphs with a structured plot to turn raw numbers into clear / actionable insights
  • Those insights help to provide answers for a main theme (i.e. the social issue / main topic you are investigating).

In the project (& workplace), it is important to demonstrate to us that you know how to organize structured & interesting narratives to present the patterns discovered in the datasets. Here are a few things that we will pay attention to when grading your project:


  • The ability to wrap up raw patterns discovered from the dataset (no matter its discovered by you or AI) into organized, meaningful & interesting insights.
  • The ability to design & organize data visualization dashboard(s) to deliver narratives on your findings effectively (i.e. Section 5).
  • The ability to present an interesting narrative / story from your data visualizations, such that users / audience can learn something interesting & meaningful related to the project topic easily.
  • The ability to explain your choice of charts and dashboard design, and how these help to structure & deliver an effective narrative.

In Lab 3 & 4, we will provide you more training on how to create dashboards for delivering narratives effectively.


Part 3 - How to Communicate a Narrative to the Audience Effectively?

In the project & workplace, it is important to learn how to communicate a narrative to the audience in a clear & interesting manner.


Supposed you have finished vibe coding the dashboard. By using the dashboard you have just created, you may do the optional exercise below (no submission required) to learn how to communicate an interesting narrative towards the audience:


  • Look at your dashboard again. Think of a few objectives of creating such dashboard, e.g.
    • I want to show the preferences of wine drinking of people in different parts of the world.
    • I want to show whether people think the price of wines worth the rating.

  • For each objective, think of how to convince the audience that your dashboard addresses the objectives effectively, e.g.
    • Demonstrate how users get insights from interacting with the graphs in the dashboard (e.g. How does the dashboard organization / filtering / choice of charts helps?).
    • Provide examples of such insights (e.g. South America has the lowest average rating on red wine).
    • Discuss the practical meaning of insights (e.g. Wine manufacturer can understand the taste of people in different places, and improve their wine quality).

Note: The points above are our expectations on your project demo / final report also!!!
